title: Would You Let AI Design Your Car Restoration?

body_markdown:
Artificial Intelligence might well be the end of us all, but until doomsday dawns, one British restoration specialist reckons AI is the answer to pre-planning its projects.


Auto Rara, based near Derby, has developed a[Virtual Design Studio](https://www.autorara.com/virtual-design-studio) where customers can drive their own car in and then, thanks to AI, visualize all manner of modifications.


“A car comes into our assessment center, and then eight controlled photographs are taken as part of that process,” explains Managing Director David Stubbs. “It then gets transferred into an AI-led studio. The studio is not just about the look of the car; it’s also about research. There’s an AI agent that goes off and conducts research on the car, the history, maybe some racing colors, and available parts. It all depends on what the customer wants.


“We can change the color, do all sorts of things with the exterior, the wheels, and the spec so that the customer can check all of that before spending their money. We do all kinds of restomods and restorations for customers, and we’re not brand-specific, so we’ve got to be able to do this completely flexibly.”


For a customer’s AC Cobra, Auto Rara’s AI agents were dispatched to gather ideas based on the competition history of the model. “It was a bare shell, and we were able to virtually build it up to his specification,” says Stubbs.


Another car to go through the Virtual Studio was a Jaguar E-Type. Stubbs describes it as a study to create a café racer—a car that would stand out at a Cars and Coffee event.


“That’s got more substantial changes,” adds Stubbs. “There’s some bodywork done at the back to accommodate the wheels that we put on it, and that was all done virtually. The other thing is the research agent goes off and finds the part, so we’re using actual parts, actual dimensions as they go onto the car.”

As anyone who’s ever experimented with AI will understand, there have been teething troubles. “AI, as you probably know, will hallucinate and add bits in and change things,” admits Stubbs. “So to get it robust and working takes a little bit of setup time, but then once all of that’s done, once the eight views are in, it’s pretty robust. Getting the secure visual is the main piece, and then the online research.”


Stubbs reckons that the system “really democratizes” the initial phase of research and design. “We’re not going to libraries or going into factories and talking to Ferrari specialists about a certain car… but we can give a flavor of that for virtually everybody because the cost of it is certainly not running into thousands of pounds.”


Stubbs says that the process can take as little as a few hours and that customers who progress with a build through Auto Rara will not be charged.


As inescapable as AI seems to be, initial renders and research seem like an effective use case. Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
